definition: The overall experience a person has when interacting with a software product, encompassing usability, accessibility, and satisfaction.
extendedDefinition: User experience covers everything a person encounters when interacting with a product, including usability, accessibility, onboarding, and satisfaction, and it increasingly decides whether software investments pay off. Products with strong UX reduce training cost, raise task completion, and lower support volume, while poorly designed tools quietly drain productivity. Buyers should evaluate UX through the lens of their actual users, including less technical staff, mobile workers, and accessibility requirements, rather than the polish of a staged demo. Task-based testing during trials, where real users complete representative workflows, reveals friction that checklists miss. UX also affects adoption momentum: teams embrace tools that feel intuitive and abandon those that do not, regardless of contract terms. Vendors measuring and investing in UX signal durable products, since experience quality correlates with ongoing feature refinement and reduced churn.
